rv.q: It is the real thing—a traditional, fantastical Broadway show—independent of both the animated film and the 1956 film with Ingrid Bergman, which are said to have “inspired” it.

"The happiest surprise is how consistently good the musical turns out to be. Smartly adapted by Terrence McNally from the 1997 animated film...with Stephen Flaherty and Lynn Ahrens impressively expanding their score...
In this alt-reality, history is rewritten, a princess finds her bliss — and an old-fashioned musical likely lives happy ever after.
Sumptuous production values and a fine cast cannot, in the end, overcome the drawbacks of the production.
The broad strokes of the familiar can still be irresistible when combined with taste, craftsmanship and a willing suspension of disbelief.
It’s kitschy, old-fashioned entertainment given a relatively sophisticated presentation, and you have to acknowledge its success when you hear the target demographic swoon on cue.
What 'Anastasia' offers instead is a procession of lovely pictures, enough to compensate for a book that doesn't delve nearly deeply enough into the search for identity that is at the musical's core.
Anastasia is surprisingly mild.
The lyrics are self-explanatory (“she trembles like a flower, but in her is a power”) and the songs (one sounds like “Officer Krupke”) are familiar.
It’s less a cabinet of wonders than a featureless box.
The show in which she appears trembles nonstop with internal conflicts during its drawn-out two-and-a-half hours.
You can’t have your revolution and eat it too.

But once Terrence McNally's book finds its feet, and the physical production gets out of the way of the several gorgeous, old-school ballads therein (including, of course, "Journey to the Past," superbly rendered by Altomare), "Anastasia" has its moments of credible emancipation.

Broadway's got a bright new star, and her name is 'Anastasia.' The 1997 beloved animated movie has been transformed into a magical new stage musical, now open at the Broadhurst Theatre, with a much-improved book by Terrence McNally, added songs from the film's composers Stephen Flaherty and Lynn Ahrens, and a star-making performance by actress C...
So Anastasia sends you, if you let yourself be sent, off on a cascade of melody and visual splendor.
Given the pleasures in this escapist fare largely geared to children, few parents will probably care

Largely set in Saint Petersburg and spanning 1907-1927, the musical starts with a dream-like prologue in which a young Anastasia bids farewell to her grandmother, the Dowager Empress (Mary Beth Peil, Les Liaisons Dangereuses), who’s leaving for Paris.
Christy Altomare is smashing as Anya, with powerhouse vocals full of spark and sensitive yearning.
For the rest of us, however, it doesn’t live up to the hype.
The show, despite being filled with some very good songs and performances, suffers from its own identity crisis.
I just can’t pretend that what’s actually happened, you know, real people getting murdered, didn’t happen and it’s all ok.
As the two lovers, Christy Altomare and Derek Klena display pretty singing voices, and otherwise show as much depth as the animated-film characters their roles are based on.
It is assured, it is lyrical, it is melodic, it is beautiful, it is dashing, it is moving and it is charming.

cn.t: Critics are mixed on this lavish adaptation of the animated film, praising its sumptuous visuals and old-school Broadway charm while faulting an uneven book and identity crisis between serious drama and frothy escapism.

sg.ra: Headout and TickPick both name Center Orchestra rows D-K as the house sweet spot; Broadhurst's mezzanine overhang does not begin cutting the stage picture until row K, so D-K sits entirely in front of the overhang line while still clearing the shallow front-row rake. SeatPlan editors specifically advise skipping rows A-C because the Broadhurst stage pushes action to the sides that front-row patrons miss.

Broadhurst's mezzanine overhang begins at row K and, per Headout and SeatPlan, 'visibly cuts into the top of the stage by row R' - specifically blocking projections and anything that plays high. The rake in these rear orchestra rows is also called out as shallow, compounding the loss of vertical stage picture.

SeatPlan specifically flags the Broadhurst's Left and Right Boxes as overhanging far-aisle orchestra seats around rows D-F, cutting off the corresponding side of the stage, and the three elevated boxes themselves 'sit at quite sharp angles' with unfixed chairs. Headout adds that double-digit seats near the aisle get only partial views of the stage.

Multiple sources (Headout, SeatPlan, NewYorkTheatreGuide) call Center Mezzanine rows A-B the second-best location in the house. The Broadhurst's front mezzanine ledge has no railing, so shorter patrons aren't blocked - a Broadhurst-specific quirk noted by both SeatPlan and Headout. Because there is no balcony above, front-mezz rows have zero overhang.

SeatPlan calls Center Mezzanine rows C-F the value pick - 'enough rake to see over the top of heads' at sub-premium pricing - and because Broadhurst has no balcony above, the rear mezzanine is not overhung itself. The back four rows are slightly shorter with a decent rake, and a Tripadvisor reviewer (Apr 2024) reported a 'crystal clear view' from the last row of the mezzanine.
